config.title: Search Insert Position

intro.title: Search Insert Position
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that finds the index where a target value should be inserted into a sorted array. You will learn how to implement the binary search algorithm to efficiently locate this position. The main technologies involved include JavaScript arrays, loops, and conditional logic. This exercise will help you understand algorithmic thinking and how to handle edge cases in search lessons.
intro.usecase: The Search Insert Position algorithm is essential for maintaining sorted data structures in real applications. You'll use it when implementing autocomplete search bars that need to insert new suggestions in alphabetical order, or in e-commerce filters that dynamically add price ranges to sorted lists. This pattern appears in dashboard tables where users can add new entries that must be inserted at the correct sorted position without manual reordering. It's also crucial for maintaining ordered user lists in social media feeds or sorted log entries in monitoring tools.

objectives: Implement a binary search algorithm to find the target index in a sorted array
Construct conditional logic to handle cases where the target is not found in the array
Manipulate pointer variables to track search boundaries during iteration
Initialize and update loop conditions to efficiently narrow the search range
Apply edge case handling for targets outside the array's value range
Integrate return statements to output the correct insertion position
Configure test cases to validate the algorithm's correctness

content.body: Sometimes you need to find where a number belongs in a sorted list, even if it's not already there. This is called the search insert position lesson. We'll learn how to find this spot efficiently using a clever cutting technique.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
• Apply binary search to find where a target belongs in a sorted array
• Implement the search insert position algorithm in JavaScript
• Explain why the array must be sorted for this approach to work
• Handle cases where the target is not found in the array
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you have this sorted list of numbers: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. Where would you insert the number 4? Think about where it should go to keep the list sorted.
content.title: Try it

content.body: Same list: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]. Where would you insert the number 10? What about the number 0?
content.title: Try another

content.body: Now with [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12]. Where would you insert the number 7? How did you figure it out?
content.title: One more

content.body: You probably scanned from the beginning, comparing each number until you found where the target should go. This works for small lists, but imagine doing this with thousands of numbers!
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 10,000 sorted numbers, checking each one from the start is too slow. We need a smarter method that takes advantage of the sorted order. Can't figure it out? The next step will show you.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The secret is that when a list is sorted, you can repeatedly cut your search space in half. At each step, you check the middle element - if your target is smaller, you know it must be in the left half; if larger, in the right half. This eliminates half the possibilities with each comparison!
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Repeatedly cut the range in half; only one half can contain the answer.

content.body: We'll use binary search! Start with the whole array as your search range. Find the middle element. If the target equals the middle, you found it! If the target is smaller, search only the left half. If larger, search only the right half. Keep cutting in half until you find the target or determine where it should be inserted.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Set left pointer to start, right pointer to end
2. While left ≤ right:
   • Calculate middle index
   • If target equals nums[middle], return middle
   • If target < nums[middle], search left half (move right)
   • If target > nums[middle], search right half (move left)
3. When loop ends, left points to where target should be inserted
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called searchInsert that takes two parameters: nums (a sorted array) and target (the number to find or insert). Return a number representing the index.
steps.hint: Use the function keyword or arrow function syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure you have both parameters: nums and target.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function that takes nums and target.

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create two variables: left starting at 0 and right starting at nums.length - 1. These will track our search range.
steps.hint: Use let to declare variables that will change.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we have our search boundaries set.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Remember right should be the last index, not the length.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need left at 0 and right at the last index of the array.

steps.title: Create the search loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues as long as left is less than or equal to right. This is where we'll do our binary search.
steps.hint: The condition should check if left <= right.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure it's <= not just <.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need while (left <= right) to search inclusive ranges.

steps.title: Calculate middle and compare
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, calculate the middle index using Math.floor((left + right) / 2).
steps.hint: Remember to use Math.floor for integer division.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You're implementing the core binary search logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you handle all three cases: equal, less than, and greater than.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to calculate mid, then compare target with nums[mid] and adjust pointers accordingly.

steps.instruction: add an if-else chain: if target equals nums[mid], return mid; if target is less, update right; otherwise update left.
steps.hint: Remember to use Math.floor for integer division.

steps.title: Return insert position
steps.instruction: After the while loop ends (when left > right), return left. This is the index where the target should be inserted to maintain sorted order.
steps.hint: The loop ends when we've narrowed down to the exact insertion point.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there! We need to return the insertion index after the search.
steps.feedbackWrong: When the target isn't found, left points to where it should be inserted.

content.body: Excellent work! You've implemented binary search to find where a target belongs in a sorted array. Remember: the array must be sorted for binary search to work, and when the target isn't found, left naturally points to the correct insertion position. This algorithm runs in O(log n) time because it cuts the search space in half with each step!
